name: information_release
description: The reader's information supply: what they know and when they learn it — knowledge states (suspense, surprise, mystery), the moves that withhold and release, the schedules that pace release across chapters, the promise/payoff ledger, and the nonfiction analogues where the withheld thing is a number, a caveat, or a source.

reader_knowledge_states.name: curiosity gap
reader_knowledge_states.definition: The state produced when the reader becomes aware of a specific hole in what they know, which they then feel a need to close.
reader_knowledge_states.example: By the third page you know the house sold for a dollar; you do not know to whom, and you cannot stop wanting to.
reader_knowledge_states.effect: Loewenstein's information-gap account: curiosity scales with awareness of the gap, not with the size of the missing fact — a small, sharply defined hole pulls harder than a vast vague one.
reader_knowledge_states.caution: The gap must be namable by the reader. If they cannot say what they want to know, you have produced confusion, not curiosity.

reader_knowledge_states.name: suspense
reader_knowledge_states.definition: The state in which the reader knows what is at stake and what may happen but not which way it resolves — anticipation under uncertainty.
reader_knowledge_states.example: She has the letter. He is on the stairs. Either she burns it in the next ten seconds or she does not.
reader_knowledge_states.effect: Holds attention forward: the reader reads to find out. Suspense is generated by *giving* information, not withholding it — the reader must know enough to fear the right outcome.
reader_knowledge_states.caution: Suspense decays if the outcome stops mattering. Refresh the stakes, not the delay.

reader_knowledge_states.name: surprise
reader_knowledge_states.definition: The state produced when a fact arrives that the reader had no expectation about, or an expectation the text now contradicts.
reader_knowledge_states.example: The lawyer signs the settlement, walks to his car, and drives to the airport, where his wife has been waiting three hours.
reader_knowledge_states.effect: One sharp jolt, over instantly. Surprise is a point event; suspense is a duration. A page of surprise is worth ten seconds of reader time, a page of suspense is worth the chapter.
reader_knowledge_states.caution: Hitchcock's trade-off: any surprise can be converted into suspense by telling the reader earlier, usually at a profit. Spend surprise only where the *reframing* it causes is the point.

reader_knowledge_states.name: mystery
reader_knowledge_states.definition: The state in which the reader knows something has already happened but not what — curiosity aimed backward, at a completed event, rather than forward at an open one.
reader_knowledge_states.example: The boat came back empty. Everything from that point on is the reader trying to reconstruct the four hours it was gone.
reader_knowledge_states.effect: Sustains interest across long spans because the answer exists and is being approached, not awaited. The three states divide by tense: mystery is past, suspense is future, surprise is the present instant.
reader_knowledge_states.caution: Distinguish the state from the genre; a memoir or an argument can run on mystery without a body in it.

reader_knowledge_states.name: dread
reader_knowledge_states.definition: The state in which the reader knows the outcome and only the timing is open — certainty about what, uncertainty about when.
reader_knowledge_states.example: The diagnosis is on page nine. The rest of the book is the family not yet knowing it.
reader_knowledge_states.effect: Converts every ordinary detail into a countdown; the reader reads the small talk as an obituary.
reader_knowledge_states.caution: Dread does not tolerate long flat stretches the way suspense does — with no uncertainty to renew, the only variable left is the rate of approach.

reader_knowledge_states.name: hitchcock's bomb principle
reader_knowledge_states.definition: The rule that telling the audience about the hidden threat buys minutes of suspense, while concealing it buys one second of surprise.
reader_knowledge_states.example: Two men talk baseball at a cafe table for fifteen minutes. Only the reader has been shown the case under the table and the clock inside it.
reader_knowledge_states.effect: Names the exchange rate between the two states and makes it a schedule decision rather than a taste one.
reader_knowledge_states.caution: The principle presumes the reader can do something with the knowledge — care about the men, count the minutes. Shown a bomb under an empty table, the reader feels nothing.

reader_knowledge_states.name: superior position
reader_knowledge_states.definition: The reader holds information a character lacks, so everything the character does arrives doubled — what they mean and what it will cost.
reader_knowledge_states.example: He tells the investigator he has never been to the coast. The reader has already read the hotel register.
reader_knowledge_states.effect: The release aspect of dramatic irony: what the gap is *made of* and when it closes. Every line the uninformed character speaks becomes a second line for the reader.
reader_knowledge_states.caution: Gaps this wide must close. Held past the point of usefulness, superior position curdles into the reader watching an idiot.

reader_knowledge_states.name: equal position
reader_knowledge_states.definition: The reader knows exactly what the viewpoint character knows, learning each fact at the moment the character does.
reader_knowledge_states.example: The door opens and the room is empty; neither she nor we knew that a second ago.
reader_knowledge_states.effect: Maximum identification and maximum surprise potential, at the cost of any irony — the reader cannot be ahead of anyone.
reader_knowledge_states.caution: The default in close third and first person, which means it is also the position writers fall into by accident rather than choose.

reader_knowledge_states.name: inferior position
reader_knowledge_states.definition: A character knows something the reader does not, and the text lets the reader see that the knowledge exists without supplying it.
reader_knowledge_states.example: She read the second page twice, folded it into her coat, and said the meeting was cancelled.
reader_knowledge_states.effect: Generates mystery and, aimed at the viewpoint character, unease — the narrator is holding out.
reader_knowledge_states.caution: In first person or close third this is a reliability claim, not a neutral choice; the reader will ask why they were not told and must eventually get an answer.

reader_knowledge_states.name: restricted narration
reader_knowledge_states.definition: The book's total information supply is capped at what one figure knows, so the reader can never learn more than that figure learns.
reader_knowledge_states.example: A whodunit in the detective's head: the reader is handed each clue at the instant it is picked up and nothing else.
reader_knowledge_states.effect: Bordwell's range of story information at its narrow setting. Makes mystery cheap and dramatic irony impossible.

reader_knowledge_states.name: unrestricted narration
reader_knowledge_states.definition: The book moves freely among what several figures know, so the reader's total knowledge exceeds any single character's.
reader_knowledge_states.example: Chapter four is the buyer's; chapter five is the seller's; by chapter six only the reader has seen both contracts.
reader_knowledge_states.effect: The wide setting of narrative range: cheap dramatic irony, expensive mystery. Multi-POV thrillers buy suspense with it.
reader_knowledge_states.caution: Every widening is permanent — you cannot un-tell the reader — so the schedule must survive its own generosity.

reader_knowledge_states.name: known-unknown grid
reader_knowledge_states.definition: The audit that crosses what the reader knows against what each character knows, producing the four cells that generate irony, mystery, shared suspense, and inertness.
reader_knowledge_states.example: Reader yes / character no = irony; reader no / character yes = mystery; both yes = suspense; both no = nothing yet.
reader_knowledge_states.effect: Turns 'who knows what' from a vague worry into a table you can fill in per scene and per chapter.
reader_knowledge_states.caution: The both-no cell is where drafts stall: nobody knows anything and the reader has nothing to want.

reader_knowledge_states.name: anticipation
reader_knowledge_states.definition: The forward-leaning half of suspense: the reader's sense that a specific thing is coming and has not arrived.
reader_knowledge_states.example: Three times now the phone has rung at eleven. It is ten forty.
reader_knowledge_states.effect: Does the work of pacing without event — the reader supplies tension the page has not spent a word on.
reader_knowledge_states.caution: Requires a pattern the reader has already been taught. Anticipation without a prior instance is just waiting.

reader_knowledge_states.name: uncertainty
reader_knowledge_states.definition: The other half of suspense: the reader's inability to predict which of the live outcomes will occur.
reader_knowledge_states.example: Either the appeal is granted or it is not, and the book has given honest reasons for both.
reader_knowledge_states.effect: Uncertainty without anticipation is noise; anticipation without uncertainty is dread. Suspense needs both, and you can dial them separately.
reader_knowledge_states.caution: Manufactured uncertainty — outcomes the reader can see are not really live — reads as stalling.

reader_knowledge_states.name: reader's working hypothesis
reader_knowledge_states.definition: The provisional explanation the reader is holding at any given page, assembled from what they have been given so far.
reader_knowledge_states.example: By chapter five the reader has decided the brother did it; the book knows this and has been feeding it.
reader_knowledge_states.effect: Most of the pleasure of a reveal is what it does to this hypothesis, not what it adds to the record. Write to the hypothesis you have built, not to the facts you have listed.
reader_knowledge_states.caution: You must actually know what the reader currently believes. Beta readers exist largely to report it.

reader_knowledge_states.name: false certainty
reader_knowledge_states.definition: A state in which the reader believes a question is settled, deliberately induced so a later fact can unsettle it.
reader_knowledge_states.example: Everyone in the first hundred pages agrees the fire started in the kitchen, and the reader has stopped wondering.
reader_knowledge_states.effect: Cheaper and more durable than suspense — a reader who has closed a question stops guarding it, which is what makes the reversal land.
reader_knowledge_states.caution: Only fair if the reader could, in principle, have doubted. Certainty produced by the narrator asserting a falsehood is a cheat, not a technique.

reader_knowledge_states.name: the open question
reader_knowledge_states.definition: A question the text has raised and not answered, which the reader carries forward as an active state rather than a forgotten one.
reader_knowledge_states.example: Nobody has explained why she kept the second key, and forty pages later the reader is still holding it.
reader_knowledge_states.effect: The unit of long-range pull. One well-formed open question will carry a reader further than three vague intimations of mystery.
reader_knowledge_states.caution: Carried too long without a touch, an open question is dropped rather than sustained; the reader forgets, and the eventual answer answers nothing.

reader_knowledge_states.name: reader complicity
reader_knowledge_states.definition: The state in which the reader has been given a secret that a character is keeping, making the reader a party to the concealment.
reader_knowledge_states.example: We watched him move the money. Now we watch him tell his daughter the account is empty.
reader_knowledge_states.effect: Converts superior position into moral discomfort: the reader is not merely ahead, they are implicated.
reader_knowledge_states.caution: The reader's discomfort must be intended. Handed a secret they did not want and cannot act on, readers grow resentful rather than complicit.

reader_knowledge_states.name: confusion
reader_knowledge_states.definition: The failure state in which the reader lacks information but cannot name what is missing, so no curiosity forms.
reader_knowledge_states.example: Three unnamed men discuss an unnamed transaction in an unnamed city, and the reader has no question to ask.
reader_knowledge_states.effect: Reads to the reader as the writer's incompetence rather than the text's design, and produces put-downs rather than page turns.
reader_knowledge_states.caution: Withholding and confusing feel identical from inside the draft. The test is whether a reader can state the question the page raised.

reader_knowledge_states.name: over-informed reader
reader_knowledge_states.definition: The failure state in which everything has been supplied, leaving the reader nothing to want to know.
reader_knowledge_states.example: The chapter opens by naming the killer, the motive, the method, and the sentence he will serve.
reader_knowledge_states.effect: Attention goes slack; the prose has to carry the reader on style alone, which few drafts can do for long.
reader_knowledge_states.caution: The common cause is anxiety, not generosity — writers explain because they fear being misread. Cutting explanation is usually the whole fix.

release_moves.name: delayed decoding
release_moves.definition: Rendering an event as raw sensation first and only afterward supplying the interpretation that makes it an event.
release_moves.example: Sticks, little sticks, were flying about — thick. Then: they were arrows.
release_moves.effect: Ian Watt's term for Conrad's method: the reader lives the gap between perception and understanding instead of being told about it, which is why the moment reads as experienced rather than reported.
release_moves.caution: Costs clarity every time it is used; two per chapter is a lot. Deployed on trivia it reads as coyness.

release_moves.name: misdirection
release_moves.definition: Directing the reader's attention toward a true but unimportant thing so that the important thing can be placed in the open unnoticed.
release_moves.example: The whole scene is about whether the will is valid. Nobody, including the reader, looks at who typed it.
release_moves.effect: The general mechanism behind the mystery genre's red herring and behind comic misdirection alike: the reader is not lied to, only steered.
release_moves.caution: Misdirection that requires the narrator to state a falsehood has stopped being misdirection. Steer with emphasis, never with assertion.

release_moves.name: partial reveal
release_moves.definition: Releasing enough of the withheld fact to change what the reader believes while keeping back the part that would close the question.
release_moves.example: We learn the money came from her father. We do not learn what he was paying for.
release_moves.effect: Advances the reader's working hypothesis without retiring it — the single most reliable way to keep a long book moving.
release_moves.caution: Each partial reveal should cost the reader an old belief. One that adds a detail without disturbing anything is a stall dressed as a step.

release_moves.name: withheld number
release_moves.definition: Naming the quality of a quantity — its weight, its consequence — before naming the quantity itself.
release_moves.example: It was more money than the town had ever seen move at once. It was eleven thousand dollars.
release_moves.effect: The reader builds a figure from the reaction, then gets the real one; whichever way the correction runs, it lands.
release_moves.caution: Works once per number. A book that never gives a figure straight becomes exhausting to read and impossible to check.

release_moves.name: reveal-then-reframe
release_moves.definition: Delivering the withheld fact and then, in the same breath, showing what it does to everything already read.
release_moves.example: He was her son. Which meant the phone call in chapter two had been a warning, not a threat.
release_moves.effect: Doubles a reveal's value: the fact is the small half, the retroactive rewrite is the large one.
release_moves.caution: The reframe must be left for the reader to feel, not spelled out item by item; enumerating the consequences is the commonest way to kill a good reveal.

release_moves.name: retrospective revelation
release_moves.definition: Supplying a fact so late that its main function is to rewrite the meaning of pages the reader has already finished.
release_moves.example: The last chapter establishes that the narrator has been in custody since the second page.
release_moves.effect: Buys a second reading; the book the reader finishes is not the book they started.
release_moves.caution: Everything before it must have been honestly readable in both senses. If the earlier pages only work once you know, they did not work.

release_moves.name: information ellipsis
release_moves.definition: A deliberate hole in the record — a scene, a document, a stretch of time referred to but never supplied.
release_moves.example: Between the hearing and the funeral there are four months the book simply does not narrate.
release_moves.effect: Puts the reader to work filling the hole, which makes their version more convincing than any version you could write.
release_moves.caution: Distinct from a temporal ellipsis that merely skips dead time: this one is felt as missing, and the reader will demand an accounting.

release_moves.name: theory of omission
release_moves.definition: Cutting a fact the writer knows and the reader never learns, on the premise that what is left out still exerts pressure on what remains.
release_moves.example: Hemingway removed the suicide from 'Out of Season' and reported that the story was stronger for the hole.
release_moves.effect: The omitted material behaves like the submerged seven-eighths of an iceberg — the surface prose carries a weight the reader registers without being able to source.
release_moves.caution: Only works when the writer actually knows the omitted thing. Omitting what you have not worked out produces vagueness, not resonance.

release_moves.name: unreliable withholding
release_moves.definition: A narrator plainly in possession of a fact declining to state it, so the concealment itself becomes information about the narrator.
release_moves.example: I will come to what happened in the barn. Not now.
release_moves.effect: Turns the gap into characterization: the reader tracks both the missing fact and the reason for the reticence.
release_moves.caution: The narrator must have a motive the reader can eventually credit. Withholding for the author's convenience is the reader's least favorite trick.

release_moves.name: staged disclosure
release_moves.definition: Breaking one large fact into an ordered sequence of releases, each of which is complete enough to act on.
release_moves.example: First that there was a second account; then whose name was on it; then when it opened.
release_moves.effect: Converts a single event into a structure — the reader gets repeated small resolutions instead of one deferred large one.
release_moves.caution: Order by escalating consequence, not by chronology of discovery; the stage that changes the most should not land first.

release_moves.name: the withheld name
release_moves.definition: Referring to a person, place, or thing by description until the naming can carry weight it would not have carried earlier.
release_moves.example: The man from the bank. The man from the bank. Then, on page ninety: Ellery.
release_moves.effect: The name arrives as an event. Until then the description does double duty as characterization.
release_moves.caution: Readers tolerate this for one figure, rarely two. A cast of unnamed descriptors becomes unreadable fast.

release_moves.name: late qualifier
release_moves.definition: Stating a claim in its strong form and supplying the limiting condition only after the reader has absorbed it.
release_moves.example: Every case in the sample settled. Every case, that is, that reached a judge.
release_moves.effect: The reader feels the correction as a small turn, which fixes the qualified version in memory better than a hedged first statement would.
release_moves.caution: Legitimate at one sentence's distance, a bait-and-switch at ten pages'. In argument, the further the qualifier travels from its claim, the more it looks like something you hoped nobody would reach.

release_moves.name: distraction beat
release_moves.definition: A small unit of business inserted at the moment a plant is delivered, so the reader's attention is elsewhere when it lands.
release_moves.example: He mentions the spare key while she is knocking over the wine.
release_moves.effect: Lets a setup be fully on the page — fair play preserved — without being marked as a setup.
release_moves.caution: The distraction must be doing its own work in the scene. A beat that exists only to hide the plant will read as exactly that on the second pass.

release_moves.name: deferred payoff
release_moves.definition: Planting a setup and then deliberately leaving it unpaid across a long stretch so that its return reads as inevitable rather than convenient.
release_moves.example: The scar is mentioned in chapter one, never again, and explained in chapter twenty-two.
release_moves.effect: Distance is what converts a plant into a payoff. Paid too soon it is a coincidence; paid late it is a design the reader retroactively credits.
release_moves.caution: Long deferral requires at least one intervening touch, or the reader will have forgotten the plant and the payoff will land on nothing.

release_moves.name: delayed antecedent
release_moves.definition: Using a pronoun or bare noun phrase before the thing it refers to has been supplied, so the reader reads forward to resolve it.
release_moves.example: It had been in the drawer for eleven years, and nobody in the family would touch it.
release_moves.effect: Creates a small, precisely shaped gap at sentence or paragraph scale — the cheapest curiosity gap available.
release_moves.caution: Resolve within a paragraph. Unresolved across a page it stops being cataphora and becomes an error the reader blames on the copyeditor.

release_moves.name: the answer before the question
release_moves.definition: Placing a statement whose significance is inert until, pages later, the question it answers arrives.
release_moves.example: Chapter two notes in passing that the storeroom had no window. Chapter nine asks how the smoke got out.
release_moves.effect: The reader experiences the click as their own discovery, because they hold both halves and the text never joined them.
release_moves.caution: The early statement must be memorable without being marked. Too plain and it is lost; too pointed and it is a signpost.

release_moves.name: hiding in plain sight
release_moves.definition: Placing the decisive fact openly on the page in a context that makes it look like scenery.
release_moves.example: Poe's letter is in the card rack the whole time, addressed and unhidden.
release_moves.effect: Delivers the fairness of full disclosure and the force of concealment at once — the reader cannot claim they were cheated, only that they were not looking.
release_moves.caution: The camouflaging context must be doing real work. Burying the fact in filler is not concealment, it is padding.

release_moves.name: double reveal
release_moves.definition: A reveal that the reader accepts as the answer, followed by a second reveal that the first was itself part of the concealment.
release_moves.example: The accountant confesses. Two chapters later we learn who told him to.
release_moves.effect: Uses the reader's relief as cover: attention is lowest immediately after a question closes, which is where the second turn is planted.
release_moves.caution: Two is a structure; three is a shell game. After the third the reader stops believing any reveal is final and stops investing in reveals at all.

release_moves.name: withheld confirmation
release_moves.definition: Letting the reader reach the right conclusion and then declining to confirm it for a long stretch.
release_moves.example: Everything from page sixty on tells you she wrote the letter. Nobody says so until the trial.
release_moves.effect: Keeps the reader in the flattering position of being ahead of the book while preserving the tension of not being sure.
release_moves.caution: Confirmation must eventually come, and it must land as vindication rather than repetition — usually by arriving attached to a consequence.

release_moves.name: unwitting disclosure
release_moves.definition: Releasing information through a speaker who does not know it is significant, so the reader receives it without narratorial marking.
release_moves.example: The cleaner mentions that the office lights were on all night, and means nothing by it.
release_moves.effect: Solves the marking problem: a fact the narrator does not emphasize does not announce itself as a plant.
release_moves.caution: The speaker must have a plausible reason to mention it. Convenient bystanders volunteering the exact needed fact are the oldest tell in genre fiction.

release_moves.name: the leak
release_moves.definition: Allowing one small piece of a withheld fact to escape early, well before the disclosure proper.
release_moves.example: A single line of the will is quoted in chapter three. The rest is read aloud in chapter eighteen.
release_moves.effect: Keeps a long-deferred question warm and pre-pays part of the reader's disbelief, so the full reveal does not have to carry all of it.
release_moves.caution: A leak that gives the shape of the answer costs the reveal. Leak texture, not structure.

release_moves.name: the redacted document
release_moves.definition: Presenting a source — letter, transcript, record — with parts visibly missing, so the reader sees both what is given and what is not.
release_moves.example: Four lines of the memo, then a bracketed note that the fifth page was never produced.
release_moves.effect: Makes the withholding an object in the world rather than a choice by the author, which readers forgive far more readily.
release_moves.caution: In nonfiction the gap must be real and the reason for it stated; a manufactured redaction is a fabrication.

release_moves.name: second-pass reveal
release_moves.definition: Re-showing a scene or passage the reader has already read, this time with the piece that was missing.
release_moves.example: The same phone call, forty pages later, with the other side of it.
release_moves.effect: The reader gets the reveal and the reframe simultaneously, because the surrounding material is already in memory.
release_moves.caution: Re-shown material must be compressed hard. Readers will not sit through the same three pages twice for one new sentence.

release_moves.name: explained reveal
release_moves.definition: Stating the implication of a reveal that the reader has already drawn for themselves.
release_moves.example: He was her son — which meant she had lied at the hearing, and that the money had never been his to move, and that the family had known all along.
release_moves.effect: Converts the reader's discovery into the author's announcement, and the pleasure evaporates.
release_moves.caution: The reflex is strongest on the reveal you worked hardest for. Cut the sentence after the reveal and check whether anything was actually lost.

release_moves.name: the cheat
release_moves.definition: A reveal the reader had no material for — supported by no plant, and sometimes contradicted by what the text asserted.
release_moves.example: The murderer is a cousin introduced on the second-to-last page.
release_moves.effect: Destroys retroactive trust: readers stop investing in any future reveal because they have learned the book does not play the hand it showed.
release_moves.caution: Fair play is a plant the reader could have found, not one they were likely to. The remedy is almost always to add a plant early, not to soften the reveal.

release_schedules.name: drip feed
release_schedules.definition: A schedule that releases small, roughly even increments of the withheld material at close intervals.
release_schedules.example: Every chapter of the memoir gives one more sentence of what the father did in 1971.
release_schedules.effect: Keeps a single long-range question alive across a whole book without ever resolving it, at low cost per chapter.
release_schedules.caution: Even increments teach the reader the rate; once they can predict the size of the next drip, the schedule stops generating anticipation. Vary the interval or the size.

release_schedules.name: cliff-edge chapter break
release_schedules.definition: Placing the chapter break between the setup and the release, so the reader must cross a structural boundary to get the answer.
release_schedules.example: The last line of chapter eleven is her opening the envelope.
release_schedules.effect: Uses the physical unit of the book as a delay mechanism; the break costs the writer nothing and buys a page turn.
release_schedules.caution: Every chapter ended this way devalues the next. Reserve for two or three breaks a book and end the others on consequence instead.

release_schedules.name: front-loaded reveal
release_schedules.definition: Releasing the withheld fact early and generating tension from its consequences rather than from its concealment.
release_schedules.example: The prologue tells you the plane goes down. The book is the four days before, and the two years after.
release_schedules.effect: Trades one surprise for a book-length superior position; the reader watches every decision knowing what it costs.
release_schedules.caution: Only works if the consequences are richer than the fact. Front-load a reveal with nothing behind it and the book has spent its capital on page four.

release_schedules.name: ladder of reveals
release_schedules.definition: An ordered sequence in which each release is larger in consequence than the one before it.
release_schedules.example: He lied about the meeting; he was paid for the meeting; the person who paid him is the narrator's sister.
release_schedules.effect: Gives the reader a slope they can feel, so the book's information supply and its tension curve rise together.
release_schedules.caution: Sort by consequence, not by drama. A ladder whose third rung matters less than its second reads as a book losing its nerve.

release_schedules.name: alternating knowledge
release_schedules.definition: Cutting between the party who knows and the party who does not, so the reader accumulates from both and neither character catches up.
release_schedules.example: Odd chapters are the investigator's; even chapters are the suspect's; the reader is the only one reading both.
release_schedules.effect: Manufactures dramatic irony at scale — every scene in the ignorant line is doubled by what the reader brought from the other.
release_schedules.caution: The gap has to close, and the closing has to be a scene. Alternation that runs to the last page and then simply stops feels engineered.

release_schedules.name: escalating reveals
release_schedules.definition: A schedule that shortens the interval between releases as the book proceeds while raising what each one costs.
release_schedules.example: One reveal in the first hundred pages, three in the second, five in the last fifty.
release_schedules.effect: Produces acceleration without additional event: the reader feels the book speeding up because their rate of learning is.
release_schedules.caution: The compression must be planned backward from the ending. Drafted forward it usually leaves nothing left to reveal in the last act.

release_schedules.name: the slow zoom
release_schedules.definition: Returning repeatedly to the same object or event, each pass supplying more resolution than the last.
release_schedules.example: The photograph is described four times across the book; by the fourth we can see who is standing behind her.
release_schedules.effect: Concentrates the reader's attention on one fixed point so that small additions read as large ones.
release_schedules.caution: Each return must add, not restate. Three passes with nothing new between them is repetition, and readers skim the fourth.

release_schedules.name: spiral disclosure
release_schedules.definition: Introducing the whole subject in a simple form and returning to it at intervals at greater depth, each pass assuming the last.
release_schedules.example: The first chapter defines the doctrine in a paragraph; chapter six in a section; chapter twelve in its exceptions.
release_schedules.effect: The nonfiction workhorse: the reader is never lost and never bored, because the difficult version arrives only after the easy one is load-bearing.
release_schedules.caution: Each return must be signposted as a return, or careful readers will think you have forgotten you already covered it.

release_schedules.name: last-line reveal
release_schedules.definition: A schedule that holds a single fact to the final sentence of a chapter, section, or book.
release_schedules.example: The last four words name the person who has been narrating.
release_schedules.effect: The most stressed position in any unit of prose does the amplification for you; the same fact placed mid-paragraph would pass unnoticed.
release_schedules.caution: One per book, at most one per chapter. A book whose every section ends on a withheld noun starts to feel like a set of jokes.

release_schedules.name: information budget
release_schedules.definition: A per-chapter allowance: how many new facts of consequence this chapter is permitted to spend and how many it must hold.
release_schedules.example: Chapter seven gets one reveal, two plants, and no answers.
release_schedules.effect: Makes release a plannable resource rather than a thing that happens when the drafting gets uncomfortable.
release_schedules.caution: Budgets are for the outline and the revision pass, not the draft — enforced sentence by sentence they produce stiff, withholding prose.

release_schedules.name: information dump
release_schedules.definition: Discharging a large block of withheld material at once, usually because the schedule has run out of room.
release_schedules.example: Nine pages in which the surviving conspirator explains the previous three hundred.
release_schedules.effect: Spends every open question simultaneously, after which the reader has nothing left to want and the remaining pages read as afterword.
release_schedules.caution: Almost always a symptom of a schedule problem upstream: the material was withheld past the point where it could be distributed. Fix the earlier chapters, not the dump.

release_schedules.name: payoff pile-up
release_schedules.definition: A schedule in which most of the book's payoffs land inside one chapter, leaving the surrounding stretches inert.
release_schedules.example: Chapter nineteen resolves seven of the eight open questions; chapters twenty through twenty-four resolve one.
release_schedules.effect: Produces a book that peaks early and then coasts, and readers who put it down twenty pages from the end.
release_schedules.caution: Detect by plotting payoffs per chapter, not by reading — the pile-up reads fine locally and only fails at book scale.

release_schedules.name: information sag
release_schedules.definition: A long stretch in which nothing the reader did not already know is released.
release_schedules.example: Chapters ten through fourteen restate the situation in new locations.
release_schedules.effect: The commonest cause of the sagging middle: the reader's rate of learning goes to zero while the page count does not.
release_schedules.caution: Word count and event count both look healthy here; only a per-chapter tally of new facts finds it.

release_schedules.name: hoarded release
release_schedules.definition: A schedule that withholds so consistently that the reader has stopped expecting to be told anything.
release_schedules.example: Two hundred pages in which every question raised is answered with another question.
release_schedules.effect: Trains the reader out of curiosity: once they conclude the book will not pay, they stop forming questions and the machinery has nothing to work on.
release_schedules.caution: Withholding feels like control while drafting. The corrective is a rule of thumb — close one question for every two you open.

promise_management.name: narrative question
promise_management.definition: A question the text raises explicitly, tracked as a debt to the reader from the sentence that raises it until the passage that settles it.
promise_management.example: So why did the firm keep paying him for eleven months after he left?
promise_management.effect: The auditable unit of promise: an interrogative on the page is a commitment the reader will remember making you take on.
promise_management.caution: Rhetorical questions count. A reader cannot tell from the sentence whether you meant to answer it, so any unanswered interrogative reads as a dropped thread.

promise_management.name: the loaded-gun ledger
promise_management.definition: The running list of every promise the text has taken on and not yet discharged — questions raised, deferrals stated, terms introduced, objects planted.
promise_management.example: By chapter nine the ledger has fourteen entries; nine are paid, three are uncertain, and two are guns still on the mantel.
promise_management.effect: Makes the reader's accumulated expectation visible to the writer, who otherwise remembers only the promises they enjoyed making.
promise_management.caution: The ledger is a revision instrument. Kept during drafting it makes writers pay debts early to clear the list, which is exactly backward.

promise_management.name: payoff audit
promise_management.definition: The pass that walks the ledger and assigns each promise a status: paid where the text plainly discharges it, uncertain where a single weak match suggests it might, unpaid where nothing downstream answers at all.
promise_management.example: The term appears twice more after its definition — paid. The forward reference in chapter two matches nothing — unpaid.
promise_management.effect: Turns a vague sense that something was dropped into a list with line numbers.
promise_management.caution: The three statuses are advisory, not verdicts. Unpaid may be deliberate and uncertain may be exactly the right amount of touch; the audit exists to make the choice visible, not to make it.

promise_management.name: chekhov's gun candidate
promise_management.definition: A named thing introduced with emphasis, in the first half, and never mentioned again — a gun on the mantel that the book does not fire.
promise_management.example: The Corliss engine gets a paragraph in chapter three and does not appear in the remaining four hundred pages.
promise_management.effect: Flags the specific failure readers register as an unkept promise rather than a loose end: emphasis was spent and never redeemed.
promise_management.caution: Candidacy is not guilt. Texture requires named things that go nowhere; the question is whether this one was introduced as though it mattered.

promise_management.name: forward reference
promise_management.definition: An explicit statement that a matter will be dealt with later — the most binding promise a text can make, because it is made in the author's own voice.
promise_management.example: We will come back to the second contract in chapter six.
promise_management.effect: Buys the writer permission to move on and buys the reader patience, at the price of an unmissable debt.
promise_management.caution: An unhonored forward reference is worse than the digression it avoided; the reader remembers being told, and reads the rest of the book counting.

promise_management.name: deliberately open question
promise_management.definition: A promise the book chooses not to discharge, marked clearly enough that the reader understands the silence as an answer.
promise_management.example: Whether he believed it, nobody living can say, and this book will not pretend otherwise.
promise_management.effect: Converts an unpaid debt into a stated position; the reader stops waiting and starts considering.
promise_management.caution: The marking is the whole technique. Unmarked, a deliberately open question is indistinguishable from a forgotten one — and readers assume the latter.

promise_management.name: payoff cue
promise_management.definition: The phrase that tells the reader a specific outstanding debt is now being settled.
promise_management.effect: Closes the loop consciously. Without a cue, a payoff that arrives forty pages after its setup often is not recognized as one.
promise_management.caution: Cue the long-distance payoffs and leave the short ones alone; cueing a payoff the reader just watched happen is condescension.

promise_management.name: promise density
promise_management.definition: How many open promises the reader is carrying per unit of text.
promise_management.example: The prologue opens six questions in nine hundred words.
promise_management.effect: Low density reads as placid; high density reads as propulsive up to a threshold, past which the reader stops tracking and starts skimming.
promise_management.caution: Thrillers run high and literary fiction low, but the ceiling is cognitive, not generic — roughly what a reader can name if you stopped them and asked.

promise_management.name: promise-payoff distance
promise_management.definition: The span between where a promise is made and where it is discharged, measured in pages, chapters, or scenes.
promise_management.example: Setup on page 12, payoff on page 340 — the longest arc in the book, and the one that gets a re-touch at page 180.
promise_management.effect: Short distances build momentum; long distances build architecture. A book with only one range of distances feels either frantic or slack.
promise_management.caution: Beyond roughly a hundred pages, unrefreshed, the reader has forgotten. Long distance requires intermediate touches, which is what distinguishes a deferred payoff from a dropped one.

promise_management.name: the reader's debt
promise_management.definition: The total expectation a reader is carrying at a given page — every question, deferral, and plant they still hold.
promise_management.example: By the last act the reader is owed an explanation of the fire, the sister, and the missing year.
promise_management.effect: Explains why endings fail: an ending is judged not on its own events but on how much of the accumulated debt it retires.
promise_management.caution: Debt compounds. Every chapter that opens more than it closes raises what the ending has to pay, and the last twenty pages can only pay so much.

promise_management.name: seeded detail
promise_management.definition: The planted object itself — the small concrete particular placed early so that it can be recognized when it returns.
promise_management.example: The green ledger on the hall table, mentioned once, in passing, in a list of four other things.
promise_management.effect: Concrete and specific enough to be recognized, ordinary enough not to be flagged. That balance is the entire craft of the plant.
promise_management.caution: Plant in a list. A seeded detail given its own sentence is a seeded detail the reader has been told to remember.

promise_management.name: question chain
promise_management.definition: A sequence in which the answer to each promise raises the next, so the ledger never empties and never overflows.
promise_management.example: Who sent the money answers into: why did she accept it, which answers into: what did she do with it.
promise_management.effect: Sustains promise density at a constant level with no additional bookkeeping — every payoff is also the next setup.
promise_management.caution: The chain must terminate. A book whose final answer opens one more question has mistaken a technique for an ending.

promise_management.name: central promise
promise_management.definition: The one commitment the whole book must discharge — the question a reader would name if asked what the book is about.
promise_management.example: Whether the conviction was sound. Everything else in the book is subordinate to that.
promise_management.effect: Sets the priority order for every other debt: promises that serve it are load-bearing, promises that do not are decoration and may be cut.
promise_management.caution: Made explicit too early it can be answered too early. Most books state it obliquely on page one and plainly around the first-quarter mark.

promise_management.name: orphaned term
promise_management.definition: A term introduced with definitional ceremony and then never used again.
promise_management.example: Chapter two coins 'settlement drift' in a boxed definition; the phrase does not recur in the remaining nine chapters.
promise_management.effect: Costs the reader the effort of learning it and returns nothing, and cumulatively teaches them that the book's emphasis is not a reliable signal.
promise_management.caution: The repair is usually deletion, not forced reuse. A term earns its definition by being needed two or three times, not by being needed once and defended.

promise_management.name: over-promised opening
promise_management.definition: An opening that commits the book to a scope, a revelation, or a stake that the body cannot deliver.
promise_management.example: A prologue announcing that what follows will overturn a century of consensus, followed by a competent survey.
promise_management.effect: Guarantees disappointment proportional to the promise; the better the opening, the worse the shortfall reads.
promise_management.caution: Openings get written last and revised most, which is exactly why they drift beyond the book. Check the opening against the ending, not against the outline.

promise_management.name: premature payoff
promise_management.definition: Discharging a promise before the reader has paid enough attention to it for the discharge to register.
promise_management.example: The question is raised on page 40 and answered on page 43, having cost nobody anything.
promise_management.effect: The reader gets a fact where they should have got a release; the promise machinery ran but produced no pressure.
promise_management.caution: Usually a drafting reflex — the writer is uncomfortable holding the question. Moving the payoff later is nearly always cheaper than making the setup bigger.

promise_management.name: undersized payoff
promise_management.definition: A discharge smaller in consequence than the setup that led to it.
promise_management.example: Three hundred pages of what happened at the lake, and what happened was an argument.
promise_management.effect: Reads as a broken promise even though the debt was technically settled; the reader measures payoffs against expectation, not against the ledger.
promise_management.caution: Fix at the setup end. Shrinking the promise is almost always more achievable than inflating the event, and it is the honest repair.

promise_management.name: promise inflation
promise_management.definition: Raising the stakes of each successive promise past the level the ending can settle.
promise_management.example: A conspiracy that grows from a firm to a regulator to a government, and resolves with one resignation.
promise_management.effect: Each escalation borrows against the ending; by the last act the book owes more than any ending could pay.
promise_management.caution: Detect by writing the ending's actual consequences down and comparing them to the largest promise made. The gap is the size of the problem.

nonfiction_release.name: held-back counterexample
nonfiction_release.definition: Withholding the case that cuts against the thesis until the thesis has been stated fully enough to be worth cutting against.
nonfiction_release.example: The pattern holds in every jurisdiction surveyed. It does not hold in Delaware, and Delaware is where most of these companies are.
nonfiction_release.effect: Buys the argument its strong statement and then earns credibility by supplying the objection unprompted rather than under pressure.
nonfiction_release.caution: Held past the point where a careful reader would have thought of it, this reads as concealment discovered rather than candor offered.

nonfiction_release.name: delayed statistic
nonfiction_release.definition: Letting a single case be felt in full before supplying the figure that says how common it is.
nonfiction_release.example: Four pages on the Ruiz family's eviction. Then: forty-one thousand households, that year, in that county.
nonfiction_release.effect: Solves the identifiable-victim problem in the right order — the reader has a person to multiply, so the number arrives with a unit of feeling attached.
nonfiction_release.caution: Reversing the order does not merely weaken it, it changes what the anecdote is doing: after the number, the case reads as illustration rather than evidence.

nonfiction_release.name: anecdote-then-aggregate
nonfiction_release.definition: The paired schedule in which an opening case is left unresolved, the aggregate evidence is laid out, and the case is returned to at the end with the data attached.
nonfiction_release.example: The book opens on one clinic, spends nine chapters on the national picture, and closes back at the clinic.
nonfiction_release.effect: Gives narrative nonfiction its shape: the reader carries a person through the abstraction and finds them changed by what they learned.
nonfiction_release.caution: The return must be altered by the middle. Coming back to the same clinic and saying the same things wastes the structure.

nonfiction_release.name: the standing objection
nonfiction_release.definition: Naming the strongest objection early, conceding that it is unanswered for now, and leaving it visibly open across the intervening chapters.
nonfiction_release.example: The obvious response is that the effect is selection, not treatment. That response is correct until chapter eight.
nonfiction_release.effect: Converts the reader's resistance into an open question they are now tracking with you, which is a far better posture than defending against it later.
nonfiction_release.caution: The debt is real and dated; a standing objection never taken down is more damaging than one never raised.

nonfiction_release.name: blind quotation
nonfiction_release.definition: Presenting a passage without its attribution so the reader judges it before learning whose it is.
nonfiction_release.example: Read this description of the labor market. It was written in 1911.
nonfiction_release.effect: Tests and then exposes the reader's own priors; the delayed attribution is not decoration but the point of the exercise.
nonfiction_release.caution: Works once or twice in a book. And it must be genuinely fair — a quotation stripped of the context that would change the judgment is a trick, not a test.

nonfiction_release.name: delayed attribution
nonfiction_release.definition: Placing the source after the claim so the claim lands on its own before the reader assigns it an authority weighting.
nonfiction_release.example: Half of all new firms fail within five years — the Bureau of Labor Statistics has tracked it since 1994.
nonfiction_release.effect: Keeps the sentence's stress on the substance while still discharging the citation duty in the same breath.
nonfiction_release.caution: Distinct from blind quotation, which withholds attribution to test the reader; this is placement for emphasis and must resolve within the sentence or the next one.

nonfiction_release.name: deferred definition
nonfiction_release.definition: Using a term in context long enough for the reader to build a working sense of it, then supplying the formal definition.
nonfiction_release.example: Six pages of examples of 'regulatory capture' before the paragraph that defines it.
nonfiction_release.effect: The definition arrives as confirmation of something the reader has already assembled, which is far stickier than a definition arriving cold.
nonfiction_release.caution: Only safe when the examples are unambiguous. If a reader can build the wrong sense from them, the late definition reads as a correction and costs trust.

nonfiction_release.name: punchline datum
nonfiction_release.definition: Holding the load-bearing figure for the terminal position of its sentence or paragraph.
nonfiction_release.example: The program's entire administrative apparatus — six offices, two hundred staff, four decades — was reviewing about nine hundred applications a year.
nonfiction_release.effect: Puts the number where prose gives its strongest stress, so the figure does the work the sentence has been building toward.
nonfiction_release.caution: Reserve for figures that actually surprise. A terminal number that merely confirms what the sentence already said reads as a fumbled joke.

nonfiction_release.name: methods-last ordering
nonfiction_release.definition: Presenting a finding first and the procedure that produced it afterward, inverting the order in which the work was done.
nonfiction_release.example: The result, then the sample, then how the sample was drawn — with the full instrument in an appendix.
nonfiction_release.effect: Lets a general reader receive the finding while leaving the technical reader everything needed to check it, without making either read the other's book.
nonfiction_release.caution: Any limitation that changes how the finding should be read is not a method and cannot be deferred with the methods.

nonfiction_release.name: reframing case
nonfiction_release.definition: A case placed late that does not contradict the thesis but changes its scope or its meaning.
nonfiction_release.example: Everything so far has been about firms. The last chapter is a church, and it works the same way.
nonfiction_release.effect: Delivers in nonfiction what a reveal delivers in fiction: the reader's picture of what the book was about is retroactively enlarged.
nonfiction_release.caution: It must genuinely extend the argument, not merely add a domain. A late case that only repeats the pattern elsewhere reads as one chapter too many.

nonfiction_release.name: the recontextualized number
nonfiction_release.definition: Repeating a figure the reader already met, in a context that changes what it means.
nonfiction_release.example: The nine hundred applications appear again in chapter eleven, this time beside the twelve thousand that were never filed.
nonfiction_release.effect: Costs nothing to introduce and pays twice: the first appearance is the plant, the second is the payoff, and the reader supplies the arithmetic.
nonfiction_release.caution: Only works if the first appearance was memorable enough to be recognized. Anonymous figures cannot be recontextualized, only restated.

nonfiction_release.name: prediction prompt
nonfiction_release.definition: Asking the reader to estimate a quantity or outcome before the text supplies it.
nonfiction_release.example: Before you read the next paragraph: what share of these appeals do you think succeeded?
nonfiction_release.effect: Manufactures a curiosity gap on demand and makes the answer memorable by attaching it to the reader's own wrong guess.
nonfiction_release.caution: One or two a book. Used repeatedly it turns an argument into a quiz, and readers who guess right stop playing.

nonfiction_release.name: finding-first ordering
nonfiction_release.definition: Leading with the conclusion and using the remainder to establish it, spending no suspense on what the answer will be.
nonfiction_release.example: The subsidy did not work. The rest of this chapter is why we can be confident of that.
nonfiction_release.effect: Trades curiosity for trust and speed; the suspense that remains is about the argument's soundness rather than its result.
nonfiction_release.caution: The honest default for anything a reader might need to act on, and the correct choice whenever withholding the answer would be a disservice rather than a technique.

nonfiction_release.name: deferred stake disclosure
nonfiction_release.definition: Delaying the statement of the author's own interest in the subject — funding, involvement, relationship — past the point where it becomes relevant.
nonfiction_release.example: The acknowledgments reveal that the study was commissioned by the industry the book defends.
nonfiction_release.effect: Whatever the intent, late disclosure is read as concealment discovered, and it retroactively discounts everything the reader has accepted.
nonfiction_release.caution: The only safe schedule for a stake is early and plain. If a disclosure would change how a passage is read, it belongs before that passage, not after the book.

nonfiction_release.name: late caveat
nonfiction_release.definition: A limitation that changes how a claim should be understood, placed far enough after the claim that most readers will act on the unqualified version.
nonfiction_release.example: Chapter three's headline effect; chapter nine's note that it holds only for firms above fifty employees.
nonfiction_release.effect: Readers who stop early — that is, most of them — carry away a claim the book does not actually support.
nonfiction_release.caution: The test is functional, not stylistic: if the caveat would change a reader's decision, it is not a caveat, it is part of the claim.

nonfiction_release.name: buried lede
nonfiction_release.definition: The most consequential fact in a passage placed below material the reader has no reason to prefer.
nonfiction_release.example: Nine paragraphs of procedural history, and in the tenth, that the plaintiff has since died.
nonfiction_release.effect: The reader either misses the fact or resents the nine paragraphs. Both outcomes cost more than any ordering benefit.
nonfiction_release.caution: Distinguish from the delayed lede, which withholds deliberately and pays off; a buried lede is an accident of drafting order, and the fix is to find the paragraph you were building toward and move it up.

nonfiction_release.name: buried number
nonfiction_release.definition: A load-bearing figure placed in an unstressed mid-sentence position where readers skim past it.
nonfiction_release.example: The study, which found a 40 percent difference between the groups, was published in March following an eighteen-month review.
nonfiction_release.effect: The reader finishes the sentence without having registered its only important content, and the argument's evidence never lands.
nonfiction_release.caution: Common when a figure is added during revision to a sentence built for another purpose. Any number the argument depends on wants its own clause, usually its own sentence.

nonfiction_release.name: withheld denominator
nonfiction_release.definition: Giving a count, rate, or increase without the base it is drawn from.
nonfiction_release.example: Cases tripled last year — from three to nine.
nonfiction_release.effect: Produces a reader who believes something the data does not support, which is the one release failure that is also a factual one.
nonfiction_release.caution: Sometimes deliberate, more often inherited from a source that did it first. Either way the fix is the same: supply the base in the same sentence.
